It is highly recommended to schedule your appointment in advance and complete the Red Cross registration online at:  https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/drive-results?zipSponsor=ritstudentrochester 
 
You don't need a special reason to give blood. You just need your own reason. Some of us give blood because we were asked by a friend. Some know that a family member or a friend might need blood some day. Some believe it is the right thing to do. Some do it for the free cookies and juice. Everyone enjoys the great feeling of helping save lives!

If you are unsure if you are eligible to give blood - check out the Red Cross Website: https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/drive-results?zipSponsor=ritstudentrochester

Deaf/Hard of Hearing Students needing ASL interpretation should submit an Access Services Request. 

About MOOG: TL;DR: MOOG designs any system that moves (especially) on planes. 

From MOOG: Our engineers have developed the capability to design and manufacture the most advanced motion control products for aerospace, defense, industrial and medical applications – applications where precise control of velocity, force, acceleration and fluid flow are critical. description:
Do you struggle with anxiety like so many of us? Join CaPS provider, Thomas Peechatt, LMHC-D, for a one-time didactic workshop aimed at defining the experience of anxiety and developing skills for managing it effectively. This 90-minute workshop combines 3 focus areas dedicated to: 1) understanding anxiety, 2) introducing a method for slowing down and disentangling the experience of anxiety, and 3) developing alternative, healthier responses. By the end of the workshop, you will have the tools to create your own individualized plan for managing anxiety.

Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) is a skills-based training course for anyone who wants to make their community more compassionate, informed, and prepared to support student mental health. 

Through this training, you will learn:

How to describe and talk about mental health, openly and non-judgmentally.
Approach, reassure, and support a fellow RIT community member when they are struggling with their mental health.
Exploration of what self-care looks like for you and practical applications of self-care.
If you have any questions, or you need clarification on anything, please do not hesitate to email Beau Gibbs at bmghcw@rit.edu.  

You will need to complete 2.5 hours of pre-work BEFORE attending the training. This pre-work will be made available to you approximately 1 week before the start of the training.

Thank you for your commitment to making RIT a more mentally well campus.

description:
About Goodbye, Goodbuy!
Every year, RIT students throw out over 100 tons of goods during move-out. The following fall, incoming students purchase the same items. The cycle continues, and usable items sit in landfills. We set out to change this cycle, and reduce waste! Learn more at rit.edu/goodbyegoodbuy.

Volunteer Procedure:
If volunteering, please go to the Gene Polisseni Center.
Volunteers must check in with a Captain. Captains will assign tasks to volunteers based on preferences and needs for the day.
Safety is our priority! All volunteers are required to wear close-toed shoes. Work gloves and vests will be provided. 
Interpreting services may be requested by volunteers for their shift through myaccess.rit.edu

Volunteer tasks:
Early in the week, volunteers will assist with sale set up. Later, they will restock the sale floor, help customers, and assist in making deliveries.

Volunteer Perks:

It is highly recommended to schedule your appointment in advance and complete the Red Cross registration online at:  https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/drive-results?zipSponsor=ritstudentrochester

Everyone enjoys the great feeling of helping save lives!

description:
Can we know the future? If so, what does it mean for a claim about the future to be true?

This salon examines how philosophy, forecasting, and public policy approach questions of uncertainty, prediction, and truth. The discussion explores the role of evidence, probability, and scientific reasoning in making credible claims about futures—from everyday forecasts to long-term policy decisions.

Speaker Perspectives:

John Capps argues that dismissing knowledge about the future undermines public trust in science and engineering, both of which rely on making credible claims about future outcomes. Drawing on American pragmatism and theories of truth, he explores how we can responsibly evaluate claims about futures while strengthening democratic decision-making. John Capps is a professor in RIT's Department of Philosophy whose research focuses on American philosophy, theories of truth and knowledge, and democratic institutions.
 
Eric Hittinger approaches the future through quantitative forecasting and decision analysis. Rather than asking whether a specific prediction is true, he considers whether forecasts appropriately represent uncertainty. Weather forecasts, energy modeling, and probabilistic prediction provide examples of how rigorous uncertainty can produce reliable knowledge about the future. Eric Hittinger is Professor of Public Policy and Director of the School of Public Affairs. His research focuses on techno-economic analysis of energy systems and climate policy.
What is the Futures Salon? Talks, workshops, collaborative experiments, and public discussion, the Futures Salon supports intellectual exchange across disciplines while cultivating new ways of understanding and intervening in the worlds that are possible, probable, and preferable.

Please submit interpreting requests to myAccess.rit.edu.

description:
Speaker: Hwan Shim, Ph.D.

Title: From Auditory Cognitive Neuroscience to Open-Source EEG/Audio Wearables and Unified Algorithmic Frameworks

Short Bio: Hwan Shim, Ph.D., is an Assistant Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering Technology at the Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) and Principal Investigator of the Music and Audio Cognition Lab (MACL, rit.edu/macl). He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from Seoul National University (2008). Dr. Shim’s background spans academia and industry, with prior appointments at Samsung Electronics (Principal Engineer), Stanford University, the University of Iowa, and Dong-Ah Institute of Media and Arts.

Abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms of selective attention to a target speaker in complex acoustic environments provides a basis for the development of neuro-steered hearing devices. Auditory cognitive neuroscience studies have demonstrated that selective attention modulates cortical responses to target and competing sounds, motivating auditory attention decoding (AAD) approaches that infer a listener’s attentional focus from EEG.

This talk reviews recent progress toward translating these findings from controlled laboratory experiments into practical, real-world systems. I will first introduce neural mechanisms of auditory selective attention and the evolution of AAD from linear stimulus–response models to deep-learning and semantic decoding approaches. I will then present our ongoing development of an open-source EEG/audio wearable integrating dry EEG electrodes, microphone arrays, embedded processing, and audio output, together with efforts to reduce the number of EEG channels required for reliable decoding. Finally, I will discuss unified preprocessing and algorithmic frameworks for combining heterogeneous EEG datasets and improving cross-dataset generalization. Together, these efforts illustrate a path toward multimodal, wearable, and adaptive auditory attention decoding systems capable of operating beyond the laboratory and ultimately supporting real-world neuro-steered hearing technologies.

ASL-English interpreters have been requested. Light refreshments will be provided.

description:
Math getting hard? Good—that means you’re actually learning. No one gets it right on the first try, so come take a breather and recharge at Puzzles with the Profs! This isn't a lecture, and there is zero calculus required. It’s a low-pressure hang out designed to help you build your academic bench for the semester. Drop in to play giant Jenga, play games, grab free food, and hear professors share their own hilarious "faculty fail" stories from when they were in your shoes.

Why You Should Be There:

• Free Food & Games: Kick back with giant Jenga, board games, and great snacks.
• Faculty Fail Stories: Hear your math profs spill the real, unedited truth about the times they completely bombed a test or didn't know how they were going to pass a class.
• Build Your Support Bench: Mistakes are expected in college, but knowing who has your back makes all the difference. Meet the people who can help when you hit a wall:

Your Professors (Math 111 and Math 171)
Recitation Leaders & ASC Math Support Tutors
Saturday Morning Math Academy Crew
Classmates who are in the exact same boat
Come as you are, bring your mistakes, and leave with a solid game plan for the term.
---

title: Campus Connect: Puzzle with the Profs

39 percent featured LGBTQ+ characters or people

- Bedazzle a FREE copy of a banned book

Everyone enjoys the great feeling of helping save lives!

description:
Do you struggle with anxiety like so many of us? Join CaPS provider, Thomas Peechatt, LMHC-D, for a one-time didactic workshop aimed at defining the experience of anxiety and developing skills for managing it effectively. This 90-minute workshop combines 3 focus areas dedicated to: 1) understanding anxiety, 2) introducing a method for slowing down and disentangling the experience of anxiety, and 3) developing alternative, healthier responses. By the end of the workshop, you will have the tools to create your own individualized plan for managing anxiety.

description:
The Injured Body is a film about racism, resilience, and radical imagination. It asks the question: how do we carry the weight of racism in our bodies, what does it mean for our mental and physical health, and how can we begin to heal?


Shot in Rochester and across the changing seasons of Upstate New York, the documentary delves into the everyday realities of racial microaggressions through candid conversations with 16 women of color and features mesmerizing dance sequences primarily choreographed by Mariko Yamada and portrait photography by Erica Jae. 


Following the screening, there will be a panel discussion with director Mara Ahmed, an RIT alum, on the complex intersections of race, gender, and identity in today’s America. All are welcome.
---

title: The Injured Body: A Film About Racism in America - Screening and Director Q&A

description:
Are you interested in applying for on of our 2027 Alternative Break Immersion Trips?

The Alternative Break (AB) program gives students the opportunity to engage with and contribute to communities around the world. Students who participate spend 5-9 days learning about critical challenges facing communities, interacting with local leaders, and performing short-term projects with community agencies.

Led by the CLCE's awesome AB team, our AB Information Sessions cover all the questions you may have about our program. Information sessions are optional for anyone interested in submitting an application for our 2027 trips, but are highly encouraged for anyone who is new to the program

If you cannot make any of our Information Sessions and would like more information, please email Victoria Cirillo (vrcrli@rit.edu) to set up an individual meeting.

description:
Speaker: Tim Bakken, Professor of law in the Department of Law & Philosophy at the United States Military Academy

Short Bio: Bakken has worked in civil and criminal litigation in New York City, at law firms, and as an assistant district attorney in Brooklyn. He has been a visiting scholar or fellow at the University of Cambridge Faculty of Law, University of Sydney Law School, Columbia University School of Law, New York Law School, and Australian National University College of Law. 

He was an advisor to the National Military Academy of Afghanistan in Kabul, where he created the Department of Law. He has been a visiting professor at Ural State Law University in Yekaterinburg, Russia, and the University of Chile in Santiago as a Fulbright Specialist.

Abstract: Interpreted by the courts as a constitutional right, academic freedom, in theory, permits college teachers to express their expert opinions so that student will receive an education that is based on a search for truth, free from influences that would otherwise limit the search. This lecture concerns what happens when colleges, formally or informally, inhibit professors from expressing their opinions in class. Sometimes, the inhibitors in this academic environment are often fellow professors, as well as individual professors who censure themselves. The lecture explores how even tenured professors and advanced students may not perceive the many variables that lead to constraints on their communication and argumentation. Learning can become suboptimal, and the consequences can be long-lasting.

Join the lecture via ZOOM.

Please submit interpreting requests to myAccess.rit.edu.
---

organizer: College of Liberal Arts Student Services
title: Measuring the Value of Academic Freedom in the Classroom: How Professors’ Opinions Affect Students’ Learning and Performance, an Ezra Hale Lecture Series

description:
Lavender Lit, a book group featuring literature by queer women and nonbinary authors, will meet three times during the Fall semester on Wednesdays from 3-4pm in PRISM (Campus Center 2050).

This semester, we'll read Juliet Takes a Breath by Gabby Rivera. Free copies of the book will be available at the Women, Gender, and Sexuality Resource Center (Campus Center 2010) for those who register. Please register to request an interpreter or other accommodations.

Schedule:

September 16th: read/discuss pages 1-105
October 21st: read/discuss pages 106-215
November 18th: read/discuss pages 216-320

About the book:
 
Juliet Milagros Palante is a self-proclaimed closeted Puerto Rican baby dyke from the Bronx. Only, she's not so closeted anymore. Not after coming out to her family the night before flying to Portland, Oregon, to intern with her favorite feminist writer--what's sure to be a life-changing experience. And when Juliet's coming out crashes and burns, she's not sure her mom will ever speak to her again.

But Juliet has a plan--sort of. Her internship with legendary author Harlowe Brisbane, the ultimate authority on feminism, women's bodies, and other gay-sounding stuff, is sure to help her figure out this whole "Puerto Rican lesbian" thing. Except Harlowe's white. And not from the Bronx. And she definitely doesn't have all the answers . . .

In a summer bursting with queer brown dance parties, a sexy fling with a motorcycling librarian, and intense explorations of race and identity, Juliet learns what it means to come out--to the world, to her family, to herself.

About the author: 

Gabby Rivera is a Bronx-born queer Puerto Rican babe on a mission to create the wildest, most fun stories ever. She's the first Latina to write for Marvel comics, penning the solo series AMERICA about America Chavez, a portal-punching queer Latina powerhouse. In 2017, Gabby was named one of the top comic creators by the SyFy network, and one of NBC's #Pride30 Innovators. Gabby now makes magic on both coasts, currently residing in California. She writes for all the sweet baby queers and her mom.

description:
Speaker: Martin Peterson, Full Professor of Philosophyand Elisabeth Scurlock Chair in Human Values of Ethics in Artificial Intelligence. South Methodist University

Abstract: This talk is based on my personal experience as Chair of the Academic Freedom Council at Texas A&M University (2024-2026). The contemporary moral issue I discuss is the following: How should students and faculty respond to institutional censorship? I will use Texas A&M's decision to censor Plato as a case study and identify four possible responses: anticipatory obedience, civil disobedience, malicious compliance, and what I call dissenting compliance. Anticipatory obedience—conforming to perceived expectations before being explicitly required to do so—is morally problematic because it reinforces and extends censorship. Civil disobedience, while admirable in many political contexts, may be less justifiable in academia when its expected benefits are small compared to the substantial personal and professional risks. Malicious compliance avoids capitulation but depends on deliberately disruptive, bad-faith adherence to rules. I argue instead for dissenting compliance: complying with institutional policies while explicitly and publicly expressing principled disagreement with them. Ideally, undertaken with a light touch and sometimes humor, dissenting compliance can expose unreasonable constraints without sacrificing professionalism.

Short Bio: Martin Peterson joined SMU’s Department of Philosophy as Full Professor and Elisabeth Scurlock Chair in Human Values of Ethics in Artificial Intelligence in August 2026.

Peterson conducts research in AI ethics, ethics of technology, normative ethics, and decision theory. His work examines philosophical questions about emerging technologies, with particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and rational decision-making.

Before joining the Department of Philosophy at SMU, Peterson was the Sue G. and Harry E. Bovay Jr. Professor of the History and Ethics of Professional Engineering and Professor of Philosophy at Texas A&M University, where he served from 2014 to 2026. He previously held academic positions at Eindhoven University of Technology and the University of Cambridge.

Peterson is the author of several books, including Ethics for Engineers (Oxford University Press, 2nd ed. 2025), Ethics in the Gray Area (Cambridge University Press, 2023), The Ethics of Technology (Oxford University Press, 2017), The Dimensions of Consequentialism (Cambridge University Press, 2013), An Introduction to Decision Theory (Cambridge University Press, 2nd ed. 2017), and Non-Bayesian Decision Theory (Springer, 2008). He is also Editor of Cambridge Elements in Decision Theory and Philosophy.

He received his BA and MA from Stockholm University and his PhD in philosophy from KTH Royal Institute of Technology.

Join the lecture via ZOOM.

description:
Be part of the tradition that connects RIT women and nonbinary students: past, present, and future!

Join us for this annual RIT tradition of over 20 years, a lantern march through campus welcoming incoming women and nonbinary students. Participants will receive a commemorative lantern with a piece of advice or encouragement from a former student. This year's theme is honoring our history while embracing our future. 

This event will begin with an opening ceremony in the Davis Room (SAU 1300), followed by a lantern march through campus, with a reception to follow in the University Gallery (Booth Hall 2700). All RIT community members are welcome. Please register to request interpreters or accommodations. 

Event Overview:
Thursday, August 27th
7:30pm: welcoming ceremony - Davis Room (SAU 1300)
8pm: lantern march through campus
8:30pm: reception - University Gallery (Booth Hall 2700)

description:
Speaker: Alessandra Buccella, Ph.D.

Title: Unpacking LLM-mindedness

Short Bio: Alessandra Buccella is Assistant Professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University at Albany. Her main areas of expertise are the philosophy of mind and the philosophy of artificial intelligence. Her current research focuses on articulating the ethical and societal implications of AI technologies within a framework centered on the notion of human flourishing. She is also interested in exploring how Large Language Models ‘think’ and whether their internal structures and processes resemble or approximate human cognition in any significant ways.

Abstract: Do AI systems like ChatGPT or Claude (aka Large Language Models, or LLMs) have minds? Some philosophers think they might. According to these philosophers, LLMs’ internal information-processing structures bear some functional similarities with mental representations and, therefore, might be seen as having “intentionality” – a notion many consider the “mark” of anything mental or psychological. In this talk, I try to disentangle the question of LLM-mindedness itself from the specific assumptions those who are open to the possibility make regarding the very notion of intentionality. Once these assumptions have been properly made explicit, I shall argue that, depending on how one understands the notion of intentionality, the very question of whether LLMs have minds is either meaningless or calls for an answer that is, at best, philosophically uninteresting.

 ASL-English interpreters have been requested. Light refreshments will be provided.
---

The format emphasizes effective communication of complex research to a non-specialist audience, typically with one static slide. These presentations promote effective communication skills, public engagement, networking, and professional development. 

This prep session will provide strategies for presenting your research concisely and persuasively. Receive tips on public speaking, slide design, and body language to ensure your delivery is confident, clear, and impactful. Get answers to questions, share insights with fellow participants, and collaborate in a supportive environment. Engage in interactive exercises to practice condensing your research into a concise format, with constructive feedback from experienced facilitators from the Expressive Communication Center 

Open to all - whether you are planning to enter the 3MT competition or if you'd just like to improve your communication and"elevator pitch" skills

Make your request for interpreter services at https://myaccess.rit.edu/myAccess5/

description:
Do you struggle with anxiety like so many of us? Join CaPS provider, Thomas Peechatt, LMHC-D, for a one-time didactic workshop aimed at defining the experience of anxiety and developing skills for managing it effectively. This 90-minute workshop combines 3 focus areas dedicated to: 1) understanding anxiety, 2) introducing a method for slowing down and disentangling the experience of anxiety, and 3) developing alternative, healthier responses. By the end of the workshop, you will have the tools to create your own individualized plan for managing anxiety.
This workshop is hosted by CaPS, in partnership with Graduate Studies, and open to just graduate students to generate a space for acknowledging and developing strategies to address some of the unique challenges & stressors faced during graduate studies.

description:
Join the Future Stewards Program at the Seneca Park Zoo on Saturday, September 5, 2026 for the first-ever Honoring Haudenosaunee Relationships Day.

FSP will cover zoo admission for participating students. Transportation arrangements will be communicated separately based on interest and availability.

This special event was created and is being led by Kanyʌhtowa·nʌ Cheyenne Reuben-Thomas, a Seneca Park Zoo Naturalist and Indigenous ecologist who is a member of the Oneida Nation and the Tonawanda Seneca Nation.

Throughout the day, the Zoo will offer educational programs centered on Haudenosaunee cultural knowledge, relationships with more-than-human relatives, and Indigenous approaches to conservation and environmental stewardship. Programs will connect ancient and modern stories with present-day conservation efforts and encourage guests to think more deeply about local species, habitats, sustainability, and their own responsibilities to the natural world.

Programming Schedule

9:30 a.m. Ohèn:ton Karihwatéhkwen | Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address
9:30–10:15 a.m. Turtle Meet & Greet | Keepers of the Land
10:30 a.m. Otter | Guardians
11:30 a.m. Polar Bear | Healers and Lessons
12:00 p.m. Indigenous Environmental Stewardship: Historical and Ongoing
1:30 p.m. Hellbender | Conservation in the Ohi:yo’
2:30 p.m. Eagle | Protectors
3:30 p.m. Sturgeon | Wisdom and Resilience
Throughout the day, guests can also visit the Nature Cart to learn about Haudenosaunee relationships with more-than-human relatives and connect with community organizations participating in the event.

The Future Stewards Program will host a community table at the Zoo and share information about FSP, Indigenous student support at RIT, and our work with students and community partners.

FSP will pay admission for RIT Indigenous students who would like to attend. Students interested in joining us should contact Kendall Scott in advance so admission can be arranged.

Come spend the day learning from Haudenosaunee perspectives on culture, wildlife, conservation, and our relationships with the land and the beings we share it with.
---
Event Details: https://campusgroups.rit.edu/rsvp?id=2332433
title: FSP at Honoring Haudenosaunee Relationships Day @ Seneca Park Zoo

description:
Did you realize that Career Fair is fast approaching (9/23)? Wouldn't it be great to get some low-stakes resume and/or interview assistance from those already in the engineering field?  WE@RIT has just the thing!

On Tuesday, September 15th, from 5-6:40pm, L3Harris will have representatives on campus for resume reviews and mock interviews with the WE@RIT community. Students can sign up for a specific time slot for a resume review and/or a mock interview; or students are welcome to drop in anytime during the event for mock interview workshopping with L3Harris representatives and fellow students.  WE@RIT has done the work of compiling common interview questions and will have them available for students at the interview workshopping area.  We will also do our best to accommodate walk-in's for one-on-one resume reviews and mock-interviews space permitting.  It is still wise and strongly encouraged to sign up for a scheduled timeslot to ensure your time with an L3 Harris representative if you would like a one-on-one review or interview.  

Note that one-on-one resume reviews and mock interviews each require a separate time slot.  Resumes are due to the WE@RIT office on Friday, 9/11 by 9am (email: we@rit.edu) for those opting for a resume review. No resume is needed if doing a mock interview. Dress is business casual, and those partaking in a Resume Review should come prepared with a printed out copy of their resume (in addition to emailing it to WE@RIT (we@rit.edu) by 9/11 at 9am. (Printing services will not be available at the event). Resume Reviews and Mock Interviews each require a separate 20-minute slot. See registration sheet for more details. 

Deaf/HOH Students: if you need an ASL interpreter, please submit an Access Services Request.
---

title: Resume Review & Mock Interviews with WE@RIT sponsor L3Harris

Join the CLCE for our January Blood Drive! Our goal is to collect 59 units from the RIT community to help meet the Red Cross' critical need.  It is highly recommended to schedule your appointment in advance and complete the Red Cross registration online at:  https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/drive-results?zipSponsor=ritstudentrochester 
 
You don't need a special reason to give blood. You just need your own reason. Some of us give blood because we were asked by a friend. Some know that a family member or a friend might need blood some day. Some believe it is the right thing to do. Some do it for the free cookies and juice. Everyone enjoys the great feeling of helping save lives!

If you are unsure if you are eligible to give blood - check out the Red Cross Website: https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/drive-results?zipSponsor=ritstudentrochester

description:
Join us for a special river cruise on the Genesee River in Downtown Rochester! We will hear from a leader in conversation at Seneca Park Zoo and enjoy a slice of pizza. After the river cruise, we will have connection dialogue and activities before heading back to RIT. 

A generous slice of cheese or pepperoni pizza is included. Additional beverages and snacks are available for purchase onboard. Due to Monroe County Health Regulations, no outside food or beverages are permitted onboard.

This talk goes into the One Cubic Foot project that the Seneca Park Zoo has conducted twice on the river. The idea is that we monitor, collect, and document everything that uses the small, one cubic foot of space over the course of a normal day and night. The plants and animals are photographed by Nat Geo photographer David Liittschwager, and DNA barcodes are done of everything collected. Through this project we can talk about the health of the river through the plants and animals we find.

This event is hosted by Rochester by Water, a nonprofit organization. To learn more, visit https://rochesterbywater.org/public_cruises/speaker-slice-and-sail-cruise-aboard-riverie/.
 
Accessibility Notes: 
Riverie is a no-step entry vessel. The boat is boarded using a ramp, accommodating wheelchairs, scooters, and walkers.

An ASL interpreter can be requested at least a week in advance. Please email E (edtpro@rit.edu) no later than 9/16 if you would like to request an ASL interpreter for this event.
---
Event Details: https://campusgroups.rit.edu/rsvp?id=2335415
title: River Cruise: Biodiversity of the Genesee River in One Cubic Foot
